transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess I’m here because I’ve been… avoiding things more than I want to admit. Anything that reminds me of my old job, really—office buildings, security talks, even networking events if they’re near work sites. I know that probably sounds silly, but I’ll just make excuses not to go.

And if people start asking about the day it happened, I usually find some reason to leave or change the subject. I’m managing okay, mostly, but it’s gotten hard to keep pretending it’s not affecting me.
Do you ever experience vivid memories or relive the day it happened as if it were occurring again?

Sometimes, yes… I mean, not all the time, so I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is. But out of nowhere I’ll be doing something normal, like washing dishes, or I’ll drive past a warehouse gate, and it’s like the scene just pops right back into my head.

It can feel very sharp. I can hear the panic in people’s voices again, and my chest tightens up like I’m back there for a moment. I know I’m not, but… it feels pretty real when it happens.
Are there specific activities or places you're avoiding because they remind you of the traumatic event?

Yes… I do, though I try not to make a big deal out of it. I’ve been avoiding office buildings, especially ones that feel like my old workplace, and things like security talks or networking events if they’re anywhere near work sites.

And if someone starts asking about the day it happened, I usually… well, I make some excuse to leave or change the subject. I know that probably isn’t the best way to handle it, but it’s just easier in the moment.
Do you have trouble sleeping or find yourself easily startled?

Yes… sleep hasn’t been great, I guess. I don’t want to overstate it, but most nights I’m lying there exhausted and somehow still wired.

And when I do fall asleep, I’ll wake up from dreams where I hear radios crackling or people shouting. Then I’m just… awake before daylight, feeling like I didn’t really sleep at all. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Do you feel guilty or responsible in any way for what happened that day?

I’m… not really sure how to answer that the right way.

I don’t think I was responsible, exactly. At least, I know that’s probably the reasonable answer. But I do catch myself wondering if I should’ve noticed something sooner, or handled things differently. I try not to sit with that too much, because it doesn’t really help, does it?

So… I guess I feel some guilt, but I don’t know if it’s fair guilt. Does that make sense?
Have you lost interest in activities that you used to enjoy?

A little, yes. I mean, I still try to do the things… salsa music, painting, cooking Sunday dinner, things like that used to really lift me up.

Now I’ll put the music on or stand at the stove and do what I’m supposed to do, but it feels more like I’m going through the motions. The good feeling just doesn’t come the way it used to. I don’t know if that’s exactly what you’re asking.
How long have you been experiencing these feelings and reactions since the traumatic event?

It’s been… pretty much since then. Since I was fired after that armed incident.

I don’t know the exact way to count it, but it’s been about a year and seven months now. I kept thinking it would settle down on its own, so I maybe didn’t make as much of it at first. But yes, that’s about how long.
Have you avoided any social activities because they remind you of the traumatic event?

Yes… I suppose I have. Not every single thing, but I do find myself steering clear of anything that feels too close to that old job.

Like office buildings, or those security-type talks, or networking events if they’re near work sites. I’ll tell myself I’m just busy or it’s not necessary, but really I don’t want to be there. And if people start asking about that day, I usually make some excuse and leave the conversation.

I don’t know if that counts as avoiding, but… yes, I think it does.
Have you avoided any intimate relationships because they remind you of the traumatic event?

I don’t think it’s intimate relationships so much, if I’m answering that right. It’s more… anything that reminds me of that old job.

Office buildings, security talks, networking things near work sites — I tend to dodge those. And if someone starts asking me about the day it happened, I’ll usually make some excuse and get out of the conversation. I know that may not be exactly what you asked, but that’s the avoiding I notice most.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy since the incident?

Yes… I guess I have, though I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is.

I used to really enjoy salsa music, and painting a bit, and making Sunday dinner. Those things used to lift me up, you know? Now I still might put the music on or cook because I’m supposed to, but it feels more like I’m just going through the motions. The good feeling just doesn’t come the way it used to.

I don’t know if that’s what you mean by losing interest, but… yes, I’ve noticed that.
Have you avoided any other daily activities or routines because they remind you of the traumatic event?

Yes… I think so. I mean, I try not to let it run my life, but I do catch myself avoiding things that feel connected to that old job.

If I have to go near certain office buildings, or there’s some kind of security talk, or a networking event near a work site, I’ll usually find a reason not to go. I tell people I’m busy or it’s not worth the trouble, but honestly it’s because it brings too much of that day back up.

And if someone starts asking about what happened, I’ll make an excuse and step away. I don’t know if that’s the kind of daily routine you mean, but that’s what I notice myself doing.
Do you often find yourself constantly on the lookout for potential dangers or threats?

Yes… I do, though I try to tell myself I’m just being careful.

Like if I walk into a meeting room or a restaurant, I notice the exits right away. I watch people’s hands more than I probably should, and I usually pick a seat where no one can come up behind me. It’s not like I’m trying to be dramatic or anything… it just feels better if I know what’s around me.

Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Have you avoided any activities that you previously found enjoyable due to fear of triggering memories of the traumatic event?

Yes… I suppose I have. I don’t want to sound like I’m making excuses, but I avoid things that feel too close to that old job.

Office buildings, security talks, networking events near work sites… I’ll usually find a reason not to go. And if people start asking about the day it happened, I just say I need to make a call or I’m tired or something, and I get out of the conversation.

I know that probably counts as avoidance, doesn’t it?
Has your avoidance of reminders or your reactions to them caused problems in your relationships or daily life?

Yes… I think it has, more than I like to admit.

I’ve turned down a few interviews because I knew there would be meetings or site visits, and I wasn’t sure I could get through them without… shutting down or needing to leave. I’ve also stopped taking on some volunteer responsibilities, even though I used to be the person people could count on for that.

And with my family, or the mentoring circles I’m part of, I’m still there, but I’m not as present. I pull back instead of leading like I used to. People have started noticing, which is embarrassing.

I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is, but… yes, it’s caused problems.
Have you avoided any other daily activities or routines because they remind you of the traumatic event besides the ones you've already mentioned?

Yes… I guess it shows up in everyday things too, though I try not to make a big deal of it.

If something even sort of reminds me of that old job, I’ll steer around it. Office buildings, anything about security procedures, those networking things near work sites… I usually tell myself it’s just not necessary, or I’m too busy.

And conversations too. If someone starts asking about the day it happened, I’ll make an excuse — like I need to take a call, or I forgot something — and get out of it. I know that’s probably not the healthiest way to handle it, but… it feels easier in the moment.
